claims.text: The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API model Expedition Base Set with a September 15, 2002 English release date; Bulbapedia also states the English expansion was released on September 15, 2002.
The local catalog and Pokémon TCG API both model 165 Expedition Base Set rows for set id ecard1.

Bulbapedia describes Expedition Base Set as the first main English expansion of the e-Card Series and says the Japanese counterpart was Base Expansion Pack, the first expansion of the Pokémon Card Game e-Card Era.

Bulbapedia says Expedition Base Set introduced Technical Machine cards, split Pokémon Power into Poké-Power and Poké-Body, and redesigned the card frame with enlarged left and bottom borders for Nintendo e-Reader Dot Code technology.
Bulbapedia says the e-Reader could show Pokédex data, play minigames or tunes, and activate hidden attacks, while hidden attacks were not legal for tournament play.

The local catalog's attention rows for Expedition include Mew, Mewtwo, Raichu, Tyranitar, Venusaur, Blastoise, Charizard, Dragonite, Feraligatr, Gengar, and the three Kanto final evolutions across holo and non-holo rows.
The local catalog's credited-artist clusters for Expedition are led by Atsuko Nishida, Hajime Kusajima, Kagemaru Himeno, Kyoko Umemoto, Tomokazu Komiya, and Keiji Kinebuchi.

Expedition matters because the card stops being only a printed game object and becomes an interface: it still carries chase monsters and artist memory, but the border itself now stores machine-readable contact with a Game Boy Advance accessory.

narrative.human_title: When the border became a machine
narrative.why_it_matters: Expedition is a beautiful hinge. The old Wizards chase language is still there: Charizard, Blastoise, Mew, Tyranitar, Venusaur. But the card frame has changed its job. The fat left and bottom borders are not just design; they are an attempt to make cardboard speak to hardware. For a catalog about assembly, Expedition is where the object admits it wants to be read by more than human eyes.

narrative.human_title: Alakazam #1 — the mind in the scanner
narrative.why_it_matters: Expedition Alakazam #1 feels like a thesis card for the e-Reader era. It is still Alakazam, still the old psychic fantasy of calculation and control, but the old Damage Swap memory has been rebuilt as Psymimic: copy the opponent, pay the cost, make the other side's move pass through your own machine. Then the border starts talking too. B-84, B-84-#, Box Topper, test print, short strip, no long strip, Crystal Pokedex text, Kusajima watercolor and ink. The card is not just a holo at the front of a set; it is Pokemon learning to make a printed object behave like an interface.

narrative.human_title: Ampharos #2 — a lighthouse wired into the card
narrative.why_it_matters: Expedition Ampharos #2 is almost too perfect for the e-Reader era. Ampharos is already a lighthouse Pokemon, a body whose tail becomes a signal over the ocean. Expedition gives that idea a machine frame. Energy Connect moves basic Energy from the Bench to the Active Pokemon again and again, Lightning Strike can spend the charge for 80, and B-81 makes the card itself addressable by hardware. Nishida's soft, light-aware hand matters here: the artist associated with some of Pokemon's deepest creature-design origins is drawing a signal creature at the exact moment the border becomes a signal. Then the variants keep everyone honest. #2 holo, #34 non-holo, reverse holo, B-81, B-81-#, and the strange pre-release test-run language are not vibes; they are separate lanes. This is the lighthouse card. It deserves coordinates.
